claim: Large-scale multi-electrode recordings from peripheral macaque retina were used to characterize light responses in complete populations of RGCs.
source: Large-scale multi-electrode recordings from the peripheral macaque retina were used to characterize light responses in complete populations of RGCs (Chichilnisky and Kalmar, 2002; Field et al., 2010; Frechette et al., 2005; Litke et al., 2004).
evidence: The statement is directly supported by citations to prior work describing the methodology.

claim: The classical RF of each cell was measured by reverse correlation between its spike train and a spatiotemporal white noise stimulus, resulting in a spike-triggered average (STA) stimulus.
source: The classical RF of each cell was measured by reverse correlation between its spike train and a spatiotemporal white noise stimulus, resulting in a spike-triggered average (STA) stimulus that summarized the spatial, temporal and chromatic properties of the cell (Chichilnisky, 2001).
evidence: The methodology is described and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Clustering of RF properties revealed multiple identifiable and complete cell type populations including ON parasol, OFF parasol, ON midget, and OFF midget cells.
source: Clustering of these properties revealed multiple identifiable and complete cell type populations (see Materials and methods; Chichilnisky and Kalmar, 2002; Dacey, 1993; Devries and Baylor, 1997; Field et al., 2007; Frechette et al., 2005), including the four numerically dominant RGC types in macaque: ON parasol, OFF parasol, ON midget, and OFF midget.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work on cell type classification.

claim: The RFs of each identified type formed an orderly lattice (mosaic), consistent with the spatial organization of each RGC type known from anatomical studies.
source: The RFs of each identified type formed an orderly lattice (mosaic), consistent with the spatial organization of each RGC type known from anatomical studies (Wässle et al., 1983).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to anatomical studies.

claim: Static, grayscale images from the ImageNet database were displayed for 100 ms, separated by 400 ms of spatially uniform illumination.
source: Each image was displayed for 100 ms, separated by 400 ms of spatially uniform illumination with intensity equal to the mean intensity across all images (Figure 1A).
evidence: The experimental protocol is described in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The stimulus timing produced a strong initial response from both parasol and midget cells, and a return to maintained firing rates prior to the onset of the next image.
source: This stimulus timing produced a strong initial response from both parasol and midget cells, and a return to maintained firing rates prior to the onset of the next image.
evidence: The observation is based on the experimental data collected.

claim: The population response was quantified as a vector of RGC spike counts in the 150 ms window after image onset.
source: For each image, the population response was quantified as a vector of RGC spike counts in the 150 ms window after image onset (Figure 1B; window chosen to optimize reconstruction performance; see Materials and methods).
evidence: The methodology is described in the text and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Reconstruction performance varied considerably across the set of test images with an average correlation of 0.76 +/- 0.12 across n = 2250 images from 15 recordings.
source: In each recording, reconstruction performance varied considerably across the set of test images (Figure 1D, ρ=0.76 +/- 0.12 across n = 2250 images from 15 recordings)
evidence: The quantitative result is stated and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Reconstruction performance was similar for repeated presentations of the same image with a standard deviation across repeats of 0.014.
source: but was similar for repeated presentations of the same image (standard deviation across repeats = 0.014).
evidence: The quantitative result is stated based on experimental data.

claim: Reconstruction performance was similar for presentations of the same image in different recordings with a standard deviation across recordings of 0.039.
source: Reconstruction performance was also similar for presentations of the same image in different recordings (standard deviation across recordings = 0.039), despite differences in the population responses and the properties of the RF mosaics (Figure 2).
evidence: The quantitative result is stated and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: The reconstructed images themselves were very similar across recordings with a correlation of 0.90 +/- 0.06, across 150 images and 66 pairs of recordings.
source: The reconstructed images themselves were also very similar across recordings (ρ=0.90 +/- 0.06, across 150 images and 66 pairs of recordings; Figure 2).
evidence: The quantitative result is stated and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The minor differences in performance between recordings were correlated with the average RF size in each recording (ρ=−0.7).
source: The minor differences in performance between recordings were correlated with the average RF size in each recording (ρ=−0.7), which in turn is inversely related to RGC density (Devries and Baylor, 1997; Gauthier et al., 2009).
evidence: The correlation is stated and supported by citations relating RF size to RGC density.

claim: The image structure and the spatial resolution of the RGC population, rather than response variability, were primarily responsible for variation in reconstruction performance across images and recordings.
source: These results indicate that the image structure and the spatial resolution of the RGC population, rather than response variability, were primarily responsible for variation in reconstruction performance across images and recordings.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing consistent performance across recordings and correlation with RF size.

claim: The reconstructed image (averaged across trials) was more similar to the smoothed image than to the original image (ρ=0.91 +/- 0.06 vs. ρ=0.78 +/- 0.11 across n = 2250 images from 15 recordings; p<0.001).
source: On average, the reconstructed image (averaged across trials) was more similar to the smoothed image than to the original image (ρ=0.91 +/- 0.06 vs. ρ=0.78 +/- 0.11 across n = 2250 images from 15 recordings; p<0.001).
evidence: The quantitative comparison is stated with statistical significance.

claim: The residuals from reconstruction and smoothing were similar (ρ=0.83 +/- 0.09), suggesting that reconstruction and smoothing captured and discarded similar features of the original images.
source: The residuals from reconstruction and smoothing, obtained by subtracting the original image, were also similar (ρ=0.83 +/- 0.09), suggesting that reconstruction and smoothing captured and discarded similar features of the original images.
evidence: The quantitative result is stated and an inference is drawn about what features are captured.

claim: Spike latency as a response measure led to less accurate reconstruction performance overall compared to spike counts.
source: This latency response measure led to less accurate reconstruction performance overall (reconstruction from ON and OFF parasol cell responses: Δρ=−0.10 +/- 0.12 across 4500 images from 15 recordings, p<0.001; reconstruction from ON and OFF midget cell responses: −0.16 +/- 0.19 across 3300 images from 11 recordings, p<0.001)
evidence: The quantitative comparison is stated with statistical significance.

claim: When a single cell was used for reconstruction, its reconstruction filter was much wider than its spatial RF.
source: When a single cell was used for reconstruction, its reconstruction filter (Figure 3A, top) was much wider than its spatial RF (Figure 3A, bottom, measured with white noise; see Materials and methods), or the spatially localized filter obtained in the full population reconstruction described above (Figure 1C).
evidence: The observation is stated and illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: The full width at half maximum of the average single-cell reconstruction filter was roughly four times the average RF width (3.6 +/- 1.4 across 15 recordings).
source: The full width at half maximum of the average single-cell reconstruction filter was roughly four times the average RF width (3.6 +/- 1.4 across 15 recordings).
evidence: The quantitative measurement is stated.

claim: As additional RGCs of the same type were included in reconstruction, the spatial spread of the primary cell's reconstruction filter was progressively reduced.
source: As additional RGCs of the same type were included in reconstruction, the spatial spread of the primary cell's reconstruction filter was progressively reduced, leveling off to a value slightly higher than the average RF size when the six nearest neighbors were included (1.3 +/- 0.2 across 15 recordings; average filters shown in Figure 3C, widths shown in Figure 3D).
evidence: The observation is stated and illustrated in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: The spatial spread of the single-cell reconstruction filter and its reduction in the context of the neural population can be understood by examining how the optimal filters depend on the statistics of the stimulus and response.
source: Both the spatial spread of the single-cell reconstruction filter and its reduction in the context of the neural population can be understood by examining how the optimal filters (Equation 1) depend on the statistics of the stimulus (S) and response (R).
evidence: This is an inference based on mathematical analysis of the reconstruction equation.

claim: For reconstruction from a single cell's responses, the single-cell reconstruction filter is directly proportional to the natural image STA.
source: For reconstruction from a single cell's responses, RTR is a scalar, and therefore the single-cell reconstruction filter is directly proportional to the natural image STA.
evidence: This is a mathematical inference from the reconstruction equation.

claim: In the case of reconstruction from the population, each cell's filter is a linear mixture of its own natural image STA and those of the other cells in the population reconstruction, weighted negatively based on the magnitude of their correlated activity.
source: However, in the case of reconstruction from the population, RTR is a matrix that shapes the reconstruction filter based on the activity of other cells. Specifically, each cell's filter is a linear mixture of its own natural image STA and those of the other cells in the population reconstruction, weighted negatively based on the magnitude of their correlated activity.
evidence: This is a mathematical inference from the reconstruction equation.

claim: When the complete population of RGCs of the same type was included in the reconstruction, the resulting spatially localized filters were similar to the RFs obtained with white noise stimuli (ρ=0.78 +/- 0.10, n = 997 ON and 1228 OFF parasol cells from 15 recordings).
source: When the complete population of RGCs of the same type was included in the reconstruction, the resulting spatially localized filters were similar to the RFs obtained with white noise stimuli (ρ=0.78 +/- 0.10, n = 997 ON and 1228 OFF parasol cells from 15 recordings).
evidence: The quantitative comparison is stated.

claim: The reconstruction filters exhibited broad vertical and horizontal structure, which is a known feature of natural scenes.
source: Most strikingly, the reconstruction filters exhibited broad vertical and horizontal structure (Figure 3C,E). This is a known feature of natural scenes (Girshick et al., 2011), and is present in the images used here (Figure 3B).
evidence: The observation is stated, illustrated in Figures 3C and 3E, and supported by a citation to prior work on natural scene statistics.

claim: The visual scene was more uniformly covered by the reconstruction filters than by the RFs.
source: In addition, the visual scene was more uniformly covered by the reconstruction filters than by the RFs (Figure 4A,C).
evidence: The observation is stated and illustrated in Figures 4A and 4C.

claim: Across both the ON and OFF parasol cells in 12 recordings, the average coverage was 0.62 +/- 0.06 for the RFs and 0.78 +/- 0.03 for the reconstruction filters (p<0.001).
source: Across both the ON and OFF parasol cells in 12 recordings, the average coverage was 0.62 +/- 0.06 for the RFs and 0.78 +/- 0.03 for the reconstruction filters (Figure 4C; p<0.001).
evidence: The quantitative comparison is stated with statistical significance and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Expanded RFs, scaled around each RGC's center location to match the average filter width, led to a small reduction in coverage (0.57 +/- 0.06; p<0.001) due to increased overlap.
source: By comparison, expanded RFs, scaled around each RGC's center location to match the average filter width, led to a small reduction in coverage (0.57 +/- 0.06; p<0.001) due to increased overlap.
evidence: The quantitative result is stated with statistical significance.

claim: The filters are not simply broader versions of the RF, but rather they are distorted relative to the RFs to fill gaps in the mosaic.
source: This indicates that the filters are not simply broader versions of the RF, but rather that they are distorted relative to the RFs to fill gaps in the mosaic.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the coverage analysis.

claim: Reconstruction using the spatial RFs in place of the filters reduced reconstruction performance by 24% (Δρ=−0.12 +/- 0.09 across 4500 images from ON and OFF parasol cells in 15 recordings; p<0.001).
source: This manipulation reduced reconstruction performance by 24% (Δρ=−0.12 +/- 0.09 across 4500 images from ON and OFF parasol cells in 15 recordings; p<0.001; Figure 4D), primarily in the lower spatial frequencies, which also contain most of the power in the original images (Figure 4E).
evidence: The quantitative result is stated with statistical significance and illustrated in Figures 4D and 4E.

claim: The resulting images using RFs instead of filters were noticeably less smooth in appearance than the optimally reconstructed images, and exhibited structure resembling the RGC mosaic.
source: The resulting images were noticeably less smooth in appearance than the optimally reconstructed images, and exhibited structure resembling the RGC mosaic (Figure 4B).
evidence: The qualitative observation is stated and illustrated in Figure 4B.

claim: Inclusion of all cells of any one cell type reduced the magnitude of the primary cell's reconstruction filter.
source: Inclusion of all cells of any one cell type reduced the magnitude of the primary cell's reconstruction filter (Figure 5B, left).
evidence: The observation is stated and illustrated in Figure 5B.

claim: The correlations were positive for same-polarity cells and negative for opposite-polarity cells.
source: As expected, the correlations were positive for same-polarity cells and negative for opposite-polarity cells (not shown; Greschner et al., 2011; Mastronarde, 1983).
evidence: The observation is stated and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: For parasol cells, inclusion of the remaining cells of the same type substantially reduced the spatial extent of the primary cell's filter.
source: As discussed previously, for parasol cells, inclusion of the remaining cells of the same type substantially reduced the spatial extent of the primary cell's filter (Figure 3).
evidence: The observation is stated and refers to Figure 3.

claim: Inclusion of the midget cells with the same polarity only slightly reduced the spatial extent of the parasol cell's filter, and inclusion of opposite polarity cells of either type had little effect.
source: Specifically, the inclusion of the midget cells with the same polarity only slightly reduced the spatial extent of the parasol cell's filter, and inclusion of opposite polarity cells of either type had little effect.
evidence: The observation is stated based on the data analysis.

claim: The spatial structure of the visual message of a single parasol cell is primarily influenced by neighboring cells of the same type and is largely unaffected by cells of other types.
source: In summary, the spatial structure of the visual message of a single parasol cell is primarily influenced by neighboring cells of the same type and is largely unaffected by cells of other types.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from the data on filter properties.

claim: Midget cell filters were significantly affected by the inclusion of the same-polarity parasol cells.
source: However, unlike parasol cells, midget cell filters were significantly affected by the inclusion of the same-polarity parasol cells (Figure 5A, third column).
evidence: The observation is stated and illustrated in Figure 5A.

claim: The asymmetry in how parasol and midget cells affect each other may be due to the fact that parasol cells tended to have much stronger responses to the natural images than midget cells.
source: This is consistent with known correlations between these cell types (Greschner et al., 2011), and the asymmetry may be due to the fact that parasol cells tended to have much stronger responses to the natural images than midget cells.
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation and observation of response magnitudes.

claim: The interpretation of the visual signal from a midget cell does depend somewhat on the signals sent by the same-polarity parasol cell population.
source: Thus, the interpretation of the visual signal from a midget cell does depend somewhat on the signals sent by the same-polarity parasol cell population.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the filter analysis.

claim: Reconstructions using just OFF parasol cells were slightly more accurate than using just ON cells, but both were less accurate than reconstruction using the two types together.
source: Reconstructions using just OFF parasol cells were slightly more accurate than using just ON cells, but both were less accurate than reconstruction using the two types together (Figure 6C, both: ρ=0.76 +/- 0.12, ON: ρ=0.64 +/- 0.16, OFF: ρ=0.67 +/- 0.14, across n = 2250 images from 15 recordings; all p<0.001).
evidence: The quantitative comparison is stated with statistical significance and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Reconstruction using just ON cells failed to accurately capture intensity variations in dark areas of the image, while reconstruction with just OFF cells failed to capture variations in light areas of the image.
source: Reconstruction using just ON cells failed to accurately capture intensity variations in dark areas of the image, while reconstruction with just OFF cells failed to capture variations in light areas of the image (for pixel values above the mean value: ρ=0.57 for ON and 0.26 for OFF, for pixel values below the mean value: ρ=0.31 for ON and 0.68 for OFF).
evidence: The quantitative results are stated based on data analysis.

claim: Only a narrow middle range of pixel intensities were effectively encoded by both ON and OFF types.
source: Only a narrow middle range of pixel intensities were effectively encoded by both types (Figure 6D).
evidence: The observation is stated and illustrated in Figure 6D.

claim: Both ON and OFF cells were necessary to reconstruct the full range of image contrasts.
source: Thus, both ON and OFF cells were necessary to reconstruct the full range of image contrasts.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the reconstruction performance data.

claim: Reconstruction using both parasol and midget cells was more accurate than using either alone.
source: As expected, reconstruction using both parasol and midget cells was more accurate than using either alone (Figure 7C, both: ρ=0.81 +/- 0.10, parasol: ρ=0.77 +/- 0.12, midget: ρ=0.73 +/- 0.13, across n = 1050 images from seven recordings; all p<0.001).
evidence: The quantitative comparison is stated with statistical significance and shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Images reconstructed from midget cells contained more high-frequency spatial structure, consistent with their higher density.
source: Images reconstructed from midget cells contained more high-frequency spatial structure, consistent with their higher density (Figure 7D).
evidence: The observation is stated and illustrated in Figure 7D.

claim: The images reconstructed from parasol cells had 50% higher signal-to-noise, resulting in the slightly higher reconstruction performance from parasol cells.
source: However, the images reconstructed from parasol cells had 50% higher signal-to-noise (defined as standard deviation across images/standard deviation across repeats), resulting in the slightly higher reconstruction performance from parasol cells.
evidence: The quantitative result is stated based on data analysis.

claim: The reconstruction performance of parasol cells increased quickly and reached 95% of peak reconstruction performance at 80 +/- 20 ms, while the performance of midget cells increased more slowly, and reached 95% performance at 116 +/- 19 ms.
source: The reconstruction performance of parasol cells increased quickly and reached 95% of peak reconstruction performance at 80 +/- 20 ms, while the performance of midget cells increased more slowly, and reached 95% performance at 116 +/- 19 ms (across seven recordings; Figure 7E).
evidence: The quantitative results are stated and illustrated in Figure 7E.

claim: This difference in temporal response indicates that spatiotemporal reconstruction will be necessary to fully reveal the distinct contributions of parasol and midget cell classes.
source: This difference indicates that spatiotemporal reconstruction will be necessary to fully reveal the distinct contributions of these two classes (see Discussion).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the temporal analysis.

claim: Reconstruction using the first two response measures (150 ms window and fifteen 10 ms bins) had similar unshuffled performance (ρ=0.76 +/- 0.12 and 0.75 +/- 0.12 respectively), and low variation across trials (standard deviation across repeats = 0.015).
source: Reconstruction using the first two response measures had similar unshuffled performance (ρ=0.76 +/- 0.12 and 0.75 +/- 0.12 respectively), and low variation across trials (standard deviation across repeats = 0.015).
evidence: The quantitative results are stated based on data analysis.

claim: With the first two response measures, shuffling had a very small and detrimental effect on reconstruction.
source: With these measures, shuffling had a very small and detrimental effect on reconstruction (across 3 recordings with 27 repeats of 150 test images: (1) Δρ=−0.0004 +/- 0.0017; |Δρ|=0.0012 +/- 0.0012; p<0.001, (2) Δρ=−0.0008 +/- 0.0019; |Δρ|=0.0014 +/- 0.0015; p<0.001).
evidence: The quantitative results are stated with statistical significance.

claim: Shuffling the responses in each time bin independently across trials had a much larger effect (Δρ=−0.02 +/- 0.01) than shuffling cells independently.
source: For comparison, shuffling the responses in each time bin independently across trials (rather than the responses of each cell independently) had a much larger effect (Δρ=−0.02 +/- 0.01), consistent with previous results (Botella-Soler et al., 2018), indicating that the autocorrelation structure across time is more important for reconstruction than the noise correlation structure across cells.
evidence: The quantitative result is stated and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In high-fidelity conditions, noise correlations had a limited impact on reconstruction, regardless of the time scale of analysis.
source: Thus, in these conditions, noise correlations had a limited impact on reconstruction, regardless of the time scale of analysis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the shuffling analysis.

claim: Reconstruction using the third measure (one 10 ms window) had lower unshuffled performance (ρ=0.64 +/- 0.14), and higher variation across trials (standard deviation across repeats = 0.039).
source: Reconstruction using the third measure had lower unshuffled performance (ρ=0.64 +/- 0.14), and higher variation across trials (standard deviation across repeats = 0.039).
evidence: The quantitative results are stated based on data analysis.

claim: In the low-fidelity case, shuffling led to a more consistent, but still small, increase in reconstruction performance (Δρ=0.0071 +/- 0.0076; |Δρ|=0.0075 +/- 0.0072; p<0.001).
source: In this case, shuffling led to a more consistent, but still small, increase in reconstruction performance (Δρ=0.0071 +/- 0.0076; |Δρ|=0.0075 +/- 0.0072; p<0.001).
evidence: The quantitative result is stated with statistical significance.

claim: In low-fidelity, high-noise situations, noise correlations in the RGC population can partially obscure the structure of natural images, even if reconstruction is designed to take the correlations into account.
source: This suggests that in low-fidelity, high-noise situations, noise correlations in the RGC population can partially obscure the structure of natural images, even if reconstruction is designed to take the correlations into account.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the shuffling analysis in the low-fidelity condition.

claim: The relationship to pixel values was more linear for the transformed RGC responses than for the original responses (Δlinear fit RMSE = −1.9 +/- 1.5 across n = 2225 cells from 15 recordings).
source: The relationship to pixel values was more linear for the transformed RGC responses than for the original responses (Δlinear fit RMSE = −1.9 +/- 1.5 across n = 2225 cells from 15 recordings; Figure 9A,B), indicating that this inverse function captured at least some of the nonlinearity in retinal signals.
evidence: The quantitative result is stated and illustrated in Figures 9A and 9B.

claim: The nonlinear transformation slightly increased reconstruction accuracy when using the responses of ON or OFF parasol cells alone.
source: The nonlinear transformation slightly increased reconstruction accuracy when using the responses of ON or OFF parasol cells alone (across 15 recordings with 300 images each: ON parasol: Δρ=0.013 +/- 0.051, p<0.001; OFF parasol: Δρ=0.015 +/- 0.035, p<0.001; Figure 9C).
evidence: The quantitative results are stated with statistical significance and shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The nonlinear transformation did not help when using the responses of ON and OFF parasol cells together (Δρ=−0.0017 +/- 0.032, p=0.001).
source: However, it did not help when using the responses of ON and OFF parasol cells together (Δρ=−0.0017 +/- 0.032, p=0.001; Figure 9C).
evidence: The quantitative result is stated with statistical significance and shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Using the raw responses of both cell types was more effective than using the transformed responses of either type alone.
source: In addition, using the raw responses of both cell types was more effective than using the transformed responses of either type alone (ON parasol: Δρ=−0.09 +/- 0.1, p<0.001; OFF parasol: Δρ=−0.06 +/- 0.1, p<0.001), suggesting that intensity information cannot be directly recovered fully from either ON or OFF cells alone.
evidence: The quantitative results are stated with statistical significance.

claim: Including interaction terms between neighboring cells produced a small increase in reconstruction accuracy (Δρ=0.0093 +/- 0.023, across three recordings with 300 test images each; p<0.001).
source: Including these interactions produced a small increase in reconstruction accuracy (Δρ=0.0093 +/- 0.023, across three recordings with 300 test images each; p<0.001; regularization did not lead to improved performance).
evidence: The quantitative result is stated with statistical significance.

claim: The primary contribution to reconstruction improvement from interaction terms was from ON-OFF pairs.
source: The primary contribution was from ON-OFF pairs (ON-OFF: Δρ = 0.0089 +/- 0.019, not significantly different than all pairs, p=0.2; ON-ON: Δρ=0.0021 +/- 0.010 and OFF-OFF: Δρ=0.0024 +/- 0.013, both significantly different than all pairs, p<0.001; Figure 9D).
evidence: The quantitative results are stated with statistical significance and shown in Figure 9D.

claim: The reconstruction filters associated with ON-OFF interaction terms typically had an oriented structure orthogonal to the line between the RF centers of the two cells.
source: The reconstruction filters associated with these interaction terms typically had an oriented structure orthogonal to the line between the RF centers of the two cells (Figure 9F,G), suggesting that the improvement in reconstruction may come primarily from using the joint activation of partially overlapping ON and OFF cells to capture edges in the visual scene.
evidence: The observation is stated and illustrated in Figures 9F and 9G, with an inference about edge detection.

claim: Simple LN models captured RGC responses to static images with reasonable accuracy (correlation between simulated and average recorded spike counts: 0.76 +/- 0.13 across n = 997 ON parasol cells; 0.84 +/- 0.09 across n = 1228 OFF parasol cells).
source: This model captured RGC responses to static images with reasonable accuracy (correlation between simulated and average recorded spike counts: 0.76 +/- 0.13 across n = 997 ON parasol cells; 0.84 +/- 0.09 across n = 1228 OFF parasol cells; see Chichilnisky, 2001).
evidence: The quantitative results are stated and supported by a citation.

claim: The filters fitted to the recorded and simulated spike trains were similar (ρ=0.84 +/- 0.09 across 2225 parasol cells from 15 recordings).
source: The filters fitted to the recorded and simulated spike trains were similar (ρ=0.84 +/- 0.09 across 2225 parasol cells from 15 recordings), and shared key features, such as horizontal and vertical structure (Figure 10A,C).
evidence: The quantitative result is stated and illustrated in Figures 10A and 10C.

claim: The reconstructed images from simulated and recorded spike counts were similar (correlation: 0.93 +/- 0.04 across n = 2250 images from 15 recordings).
source: The reconstructed images themselves were also similar (correlation between images reconstructed from simulated and recorded spike counts: 0.93 +/- 0.04 across n = 2250 images from 15 recordings; Figure 10B,C)
evidence: The quantitative result is stated and illustrated in Figures 10B and 10C.

claim: The reconstruction performance from simulated and recorded spike counts was similar (simulated: ρ=0.79 +/- 0.11; recorded: ρ=0.78 +/- 0.11; Δρ=−0.003 +/- 0.03).
source: as was the reconstruction performance (simulated: ρ=0.79 +/- 0.11; recorded: ρ=0.78 +/- 0.11; Δρ=−0.003 +/- 0.03; across 2250 images from 15 recordings; Figure 10C).
evidence: The quantitative results are stated and shown in Figure 10C.

claim: The simulated spike trains replicated the structure of nonlinear interactions between cells.
source: The simulated spike trains also replicated the structure of nonlinear interactions between cells.
evidence: This is an observation based on the analysis of interaction filters.

claim: The spatial reconstruction filter corresponding to the interaction term between nearby ON and OFF cells was oriented and qualitatively similar to the interaction filters obtained with real data.
source: The spatial reconstruction filter corresponding to the interaction term between nearby ON and OFF cells was oriented and qualitatively similar to the interaction filters obtained with real data (Figure 9E,F).
evidence: The observation is stated and illustrated in Figures 9E and 9F.

claim: Responses simulated using a linear model without any response rectification did not produce oriented interaction filters.
source: However, this was not the case for responses simulated using a linear model without any response rectification (not shown) – in this case, the filter corresponding to the interaction term had no clear structure.
evidence: The observation is stated based on simulation results.

claim: Some degree of nonlinear encoding is necessary to explain the oriented interaction filters observed in the data.
source: The model reveals that although the visual messages of RGCs depend on their spatial and cell-type specific organization, as well as the statistics of the stimulus, their essential structure can be understood using simple models of RGC encoding. Furthermore, some degree of nonlinear encoding is necessary to explain the oriented interaction filters observed in the data.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of linear and nonlinear models.

claim: The spatial filter from spatiotemporal reconstruction was highly correlated with the spatial reconstruction filters obtained from flashed images (ρ=0.87 +/- 0.07, n = 351 parasol cells from three recordings).
source: This spatial filter was highly correlated with the spatial reconstruction filters of the same cells obtained in the preceding analysis with flashed images (ρ=0.87 +/- 0.07, n = 351 parasol cells from three recordings; Figure 11B).
evidence: The quantitative result is stated and shown in Figure 11B.

claim: The dynamic filters were approximately space-time separable (explained variance from first principal component = 0.85 +/- 0.13).
source: The dynamic filters were approximately space-time separable (explained variance from first principal component = 0.85 +/- 0.13).
evidence: The quantitative result is stated based on data analysis.

claim: The large fraction of variance explained by a space-time separable filter suggests that the essential spatial features of the visual message observed in spatial reconstructions largely extend to spatiotemporal vision.
source: The large fraction of variance explained by a space-time separable filter suggests that the essential spatial features of the visual message observed in spatial reconstructions largely extend to spatiotemporal vision.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the separability analysis.

claim: The reconstructed movie frames were similar to reconstructions of static images (between static reconstruction and average reconstructed frame: ρ=0.72 +/- 0.19 across 120 images from three recordings).
source: In addition, the reconstructed movie frames were similar to reconstructions of static images (between static reconstruction and average reconstructed frame: ρ=0.72 +/- 0.19 across 120 images from three recordings, Figure 11C).
evidence: The quantitative result is stated and shown in Figure 11C.

claim: Eyes were enucleated from terminally anesthetized macaques used by other researchers in accordance with institutional guidelines for the care and use of animals.
source: Briefly, eyes were enucleated from terminally anesthetized macaques used by other researchers in accordance with institutional guidelines for the care and use of animals.
evidence: The experimental procedure is described.

claim: Pieces of retina roughly 3 mm in diameter and ranging in eccentricity from 7 to 17 mm were placed RGC side down on a planar array consisting of 512 extracellular microelectrodes.
source: In dim light, pieces of retina roughly 3 mm in diameter and ranging in eccentricity from 7 to 17 mm (6–12 mm temporal equivalent eccentricity; Chichilnisky and Kalmar, 2002) or 29-56 degrees (Dacey and Petersen, 1992; Perry and Cowey, 1985), were placed RGC side down on a planar array consisting of 512 extracellular microelectrodes covering a 1.8 mm × 0.9 mm region (roughly 4 × 8° visual field angle).
evidence: The experimental procedure is described with citations for eccentricity conversions.

claim: The visual stimulus was produced by a 120 Hz, gamma-corrected, CRT monitor, which was optically reduced and projected through the mostly-transparent array onto the retina at low photopic light levels.
source: The visual stimulus was produced by a 120 Hz, gamma-corrected, CRT monitor (Sony Trinitron Multiscan E100; Sony, Tokyo, Japan), which was optically reduced and projected through the mostly-transparent array onto the retina at low photopic light levels (2000, 1800, and 800 isomerizations per second for the L, M, and S cones respectively at 50% illumination; see Field et al., 2009, Field et al., 2010).
evidence: The experimental setup is described with citations for light level measurements.

claim: A 30-minute spatiotemporal white noise stimulus was used to characterize RGC responses and to periodically assess recording quality.
source: A 30-minutespatiotemporal white noise stimulus was used to characterize RGC responses and to periodically assess recording quality (Chichilnisky, 2001).
evidence: The experimental procedure is described with a citation.

claim: Natural images from the ImageNet database were converted to grayscale values with a mean image intensity of 0.45 on a scale of 0 to 1.
